title: Pritha calls the sun
hook: a girl in a king's house is given a mantra by a sage, tries it on the rising sun, and the sun answers
carry: the sun, greeted as a god each morning
tomorrow: a baby, a basket, and a river.

segments.voice: Yesterday: poison at the river, and a boy who came home stronger among the Nagas. Matsarya: envy, one of the six enemies.

Two days ago, Kunti told Pandu about a sage's mantra, and held one piece back. Today the poem steps back in time to tell it. Before Kunti was a queen, she was a girl called Pritha, raised in the house of a king named Kuntibhoja. When the sage Durvasa came as a guest, the hard work of looking after him fell to her, and she did it well. His gift was the mantra. Now she is young, unmarried, alone with words that can summon a god.
screen: `THE PIECE KUNTI HELD BACK.` → `PRITHA, IN KUNTIBHOJA'S HOUSE.` → `DURVASA'S GIFT: A MANTRA.`

segments.voice: With the mantra, Durvasa told her, she could call any god, and that god would give her a son. Then he left. And the text says that, out of curiosity, she tries it. She looks at the rising sun and speaks the words. And Surya, the sun god, comes. Pritha is frightened. She says she only wanted to see if the gift worked, and asks him to go. Surya answers that a god called by this mantra can't return for nothing. A son will be born. But he promises she'll remain a maiden, her honor kept. So before the five brothers, Kunti had a son, the son of the sun. Nobody in the palace knows. Notice who answered her. Not a far-off idea: the sun, right in front of her. Hindus have honored Surya as a god since the Vedas. One of the most famous Vedic prayers, the Gayatri mantra, is addressed to the sun as Savitr, the one who rouses. Many Hindus still begin the day facing the rising sun, offering water from a small pot, some saying the Gayatri as they pour. Others do Surya namaskar, the sun salutation. The teaching inside it: the light that wakes you, warms the earth and grows your food is a gift, and the right answer to a gift is a greeting. Pritha's story adds the warning: sacred things answer, so handle them with care. Today, it's ten seconds at a window in the morning, thanking the light before you check your phone.
screen: `SHE TRIES IT ON THE SUN.` · `A SON WILL BE BORN.` · `SURYA, HONORED SINCE THE VEDAS.` · `GAYATRI: A PRAYER TO THE SUN.` · then, large: `THE SUN, GREETED EACH MORNING.`

segments.voice: Face a window, or wherever the light comes in. Put your palms together, the way many Hindus greet the morning sun, and thank the light: for waking you, for warming the earth, for your food. If you pray, greet Surya by name. If it's morning and you have water nearby, some Hindus pour a little toward the sun as an offering. If you don't pray, just feel the light on your face.
Karna's abandonment. It begins here: the son the sun promised Pritha will be Karna, and what she does next follows him all his life.
Your line: the sun, greeted as a god each morning. Surya answered a girl's call. That's day seven hundred twenty-eight.
